title: Understanding grog and its uses
subtitle: What grog is, why it is added to clay, and how it affects hand-building and throwing
excerpt: Grog is pre-fired ground clay: kiln-fired ceramics crushed to a coarse powder and added to unfired clay bodies. It reduces shrinkage, increases resistance to cracking during drying and firing, and gives clay a rough, toothy texture that makes large hand-built forms easier to control. This tutorial covers what grog does, the different grades, and when to choose a grogged clay body.
sourceNotes: Grog properties and use cases synthesised from standard ceramics technical reference. Properties derived from the effect of pre-fired refractory particles on clay body behaviour during drying and firing.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pre-fired, ground clay particles added to a clay body to reduce shrinkage and improve resistance to cracking. Also called chamotte.
The reduction in size a clay body undergoes from wet to fired. Grog reduces shrinkage by replacing some of the shrinking raw clay with already-fired particles.
The drying stage where clay is firm but not fully dry: grogged clay is easier to trim at this stage.

Grog grades

Grog is sold in grades by particle size, typically described as fine, medium, or coarse (or in mesh sizes: 80-mesh is fine; 20-mesh is coarse). The grade determines the surface texture of the clay body and how it handles:

Fine grog (80-mesh and above): feels sandy. Suitable for throwing and for pieces with fine decorative surface work where a rough texture would interfere. Lower crack-resistance benefit than coarse grog.
Medium grog (40 to 60-mesh): general-purpose for hand-building. Gives grip in the hand, reduces cracking in slabs and coil work, still allows reasonable surface finishing.

Coarse grog (under 30-mesh): visible particles on the surface. Used for large sculptural work, outdoor planters, and pieces where a deliberately rough or speckled texture is wanted. Uncomfortable on the hands when throwing.
When to choose grogged clay
Large hand-built forms: anything over 25 cm tall or with walls thicker than 10 mm benefits from grog. The particles help moisture escape evenly from thick sections.

Grog particles are pre-fired clay. They do not shrink when added to a wet clay body, because they are already fired. They act as anchors in the clay matrix. As the raw clay around them dries and shrinks, the grog holds it steady. This reduces overall shrinkage. It also creates a rough, open texture that lets moisture escape more evenly from thick sections. Uneven drying is the main cause of cracking in large forms.
Sculptural work where thin sections meet thick: grog equalises drying rates across varying wall thickness, reducing the stress at joints between thick and thin sections.
Raku firing: raku requires clay that can withstand thermal shock: rapid heating and cooling. Grogged raku clay bodies are specifically formulated for this.
When NOT to choose grogged clay
Fine thrown forms (mugs, bowls, vases): medium to fine-grog or no-grog clay is easier to throw thinly. Coarse grog tears the clay walls as they are drawn upward.
Pieces with decorative slipwork or paintwork where a smooth surface is needed: coarse grog prevents a smooth surface finish even after sponging.

At leather-hard stage
Grogged clay at the
leather-hard

stage is firmer than no-grog clay at the same moisture level. The grog particles support the clay matrix as it dries. This helps with trimming large forms. Grogged clay holds its shape better on the wheel. The trimming window is slightly shorter, though. The clay becomes too hard to cut more quickly than no-grog clay.

rows.problem: Clay body seems much coarser and rougher than expected from the label
rows.cause: Commercial grogged clays vary significantly between suppliers; "medium grog" from one supplier may be equivalent to "coarse" from another
rows.fix: Order a sample quantity before committing to a large supply. Test: roll a small slab by hand: if the grog particles catch the skin uncomfortably on the palm, it is too coarse for comfortable throwing.

rows.problem: Large grogged piece still cracking during drying
rows.cause: Grog content is insufficient; wall thickness still uneven; or drying too fast
rows.fix: Grog helps but does not eliminate cracking from uneven thickness or rapid drying. Keep even wall thickness and slow-dry under plastic.
